Juvenile Mooneye (Hiodon tergisus) emerging from their yolk-sac larval phase begin exogenous feeding once the mouth gapes and the yolk reserves are fully resorbed, typically reaching approximately 0.85 centimeters [Lb = approximately 0.85 centimeters] in total length at the moment of first feeding. Field surveys conducted in the Mississippi River basin indicate that under the prevailing thermal regime of 12 °C [T = 12 °C], these young-of-year individuals experience rapid somatic growth, attaining a mean total length of 20 centimeters  by the completion of their first growing season. This initial growth increment is substantial relative to the size at hatching, reflecting a period of intense feeding activity on zooplankton and aquatic insects that fuels the transition from a prolarval to a juvenile body plan. The observed relationship between birth length and first-year length is consistent with the ontogenetic trajectories reported for other hiodontid fishes, although intraspecific variation in local growth rates is evident and appears linked to prey availability.

As the fish approach their asymptotic body dimensions, the ultimate total length recorded for Mooneye populations in lotic environments is approximately 29.8 centimeters [Li = approximately 29.8 centimeters], a figure derived from extensive mark-recapture studies and aged specimens. This value is notably below the maximum of 47 centimeters reported by FishBase, suggesting that the populations sampled may experience growth constraints imposed by cooler water temperatures or higher metabolic costs associated with their native riverine habitats. At the typical environmental temperature of 12 °C [T = 12 °C], the corresponding ultimate wet weight of a fully grown adult is estimated at 226 grams [Wwi = 226 grams], though individual body masses can vary considerably with seasonal fat deposition and reproductive status. The disparity between the local asymptotic weight and the species-wide maximum of 907 grams underscores the importance of habitat-specific resource availability in shaping life-history outcomes, with slower-growing individuals in oligotrophic systems tending toward smaller final sizes.

Reproductive investment in Hiodon tergisus is characterized by moderate fecundity coupled with a protracted spawning period. In populations inhabiting the upper Mississippi drainage under a thermal regimen of 12 °C [T = 12 °C], gravid females produce a single cohort of approximately 55 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 55 eggs per spawning event] each annual cycle, with evidence of a single spawning event per year [F_R_i = single spawning event per year]. This annual reproductive tactic contrasts with the iteroparous strategy of many congeneric species, which may exhibit multiple spawning bouts within a season. The maximum reproductive output is thus approximately 55 eggs per year [Ri = approximately 55 eggs per year], a relatively modest clutch that aligns with the species' occupation of a seasonal temperate-zone niche where synchronized gamete release coincides with spring thermal cues and rising zooplankton densities for larval nutrition.

The onset of reproductive competence in Mooneye proceeds gradually and is tightly linked to thermal history. Longitudinal tagging data indicate that at a water temperature of 12 °C [T = 12 °C], the time elapsed since hatching at first reproduction is approximately 4 years [tR = approximately 4 years], marking a relatively late maturation schedule for a fish of this body size. This delay likely reflects the time required to accumulate sufficient somatic reserves and to attain the gonadosomatic index necessary for vitellogenesis, as oocyte development in hiodontids is energetically demanding. In contrast, the absolute maximum lifespan documented for the species under these same thermal conditions extends to 11 years [am = 11 years], suggesting that adults enjoy a post-maturational period of roughly seven years during which they can contribute to the population's reproductive output across multiple spawning seasons at a temperature of 12 °C [T = 12 °C]. This longevity, combined with a relatively late age at first spawning, positions Hiodon tergisus as a moderately K-selected strategist among its clupeiform relatives.

Comparative analyses of life-history traits across the Hiodontidae family reveal that the Mooneye exhibits a distinctive combination of slow maturation and extended post-reproductive longevity relative to the congeneric goldeye (Hiodon alosoides), which tends to mature earlier and experience higher natural mortality rates. Allometric scaling of the ultimate wet weight of 226 grams [Wwi = 226 grams] for Hiodon tergisus against its documented ultimate total length of 29.8 centimeters [Li = 29.8 centimeters] yields a condition factor consistent with a fusiform, laterally compressed body shape typical of pelagic riverine foragers. Physiological studies suggest that the peak feeding rate of adult Mooneye is sustained at water temperatures approximating 12 °C, a temperature at which both the metabolic demands of locomotion and the rate of prey digestion are optimized for the cold-temperate streams they inhabit. The interplay among these demographic parameters, from the modest length at first feeding of 0.85 centimeters [Lb = 0.85 centimeters] to the terminal size and longevity constraints, defines a life-history syndrome well suited to the seasonally variable but resource-predictable environments of the Mississippi and Ohio River watersheds.
